title: Classification & Logistic Regression
oneLiner: Turning a weighted score into a probability, choosing the best boundary, and judging a classifier honestly.

what.html:
Classification means putting things into categories: job offered or not, spam or not, which of three species. Logistic regression is the classic way to do it: compute a weighted score from the inputs, then squash that score into a probability between 0 and 1.

Everyday versionAn interview panel gives points for grades and test scores. The total is turned into "chance of an offer". Above 50%, they say yes. Logistic regression is that panel, with the points learned from past decisions.

why.html:
• A straight line fit to 0/1 answers breaks. It predicts values below 0 and above 1, and one far-away example can drag the whole line and move the decision point.
  • We usually want a probability, not just a label: "70% chance" is more useful than "yes".
  • Mistakes have different costs. Missing a disease is worse than a false alarm; marking real mail as spam is worse than letting one spam through. Evaluation must reflect that.

how.title: The best rule picks the most likely class
how.html: Imagine two overlapping bell curves: CGPA of candidates who got offers and of those who didn't. Any cut-off makes some mistakes where the curves overlap. The fewest mistakes happen when each candidate is assigned to whichever class is more probable for their CGPA.

how.title: Two ways to build a classifier
how.html:
• Generative: learn what each class looks like (its distribution), then ask which class most likely produced this point. Naïve Bayes works this way.
  • Discriminative: learn the boundary between classes directly. Logistic regression, SVMs, decision trees, nearest neighbours.

how.title: Why not just draw a regression line?
how.html: Fit an ordinary line to 0/1 labels and threshold it at 0.5. Then add one more "yes" example far to the right. The line tilts and the threshold moves, so now some earlier points are misclassified. The S-shaped logistic curve doesn't have this problem.

how.title: The sigmoid squashes any score into 0–1
how.html:
Score z = weight × CGPA + weight × IQ + bias. The sigmoid turns z into a probability: very negative → close to 0, zero → exactly 0.5, very positive → close to 1.

So the rule "probability ≥ 0.5" is the same as "score ≥ 0". The points where the score is exactly 0 form the decision boundary: a straight line, or a curve if you feed in squared features.

how.title: Scoring mistakes: cross-entropy
how.html: When the answer is "yes", the cost is small if you predicted 0.99, and enormous if you predicted 0.01. Confident wrong answers are punished hardest. This "log loss" also gives a single smooth bowl to roll down, unlike squared error with a sigmoid, which would be bumpy.

how.title: Learning the weights
how.html: Same gradient descent as linear regression: predict, compare with the truth, nudge each weight by (prediction − truth) × input, repeat. The update formula looks identical; only the prediction function changed.

how.title: Reading the weights
how.html:
Each weight changes the log-odds. If the CGPA weight is 0.3, every extra CGPA point multiplies the odds of an offer by e0.3 ≈ 1.35, i.e. 35% higher odds.

To avoid overfitting, add a penalty on large weights (as in regression). In scikit-learn the knob is C, the inverse: a bigger C means less regularisation.

how.title: The confusion matrix
how.html:
Four outcomes: true positives (caught), false negatives (missed), false positives (false alarms), true negatives (correctly ignored).

  • Precision: of everything flagged, how much was right?
  • Recall: of everything that mattered, how much did we catch?
  • F1: a single score balancing both.

how.title: Why accuracy can lie
how.html: If 990 of 1,000 cases are "No", a model that always says "No" scores 99% accuracy while catching nothing. With rare classes (fraud, intrusion, disease) look at recall, precision and F1 instead, and fix the imbalance with synthetic samples (SMOTE), different metrics, or different algorithms.

how.title: ROC curves: every threshold at once
how.html: Lowering the threshold catches more positives but raises false alarms. The ROC curve plots that trade-off: true-positive rate against false-positive rate for every threshold. A perfect model hugs the top-left corner; random guessing is the diagonal. The area under the curve (AUC) sums it up: 1 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing.

how.title: More than two classes
how.html: One-vs-rest: train one yes/no model per class ("triangle or not?") and pick the class whose model is most confident. One-vs-one: train a model for every pair of classes, N(N−1)/2 in total, and let them vote.

demo.html: Train logistic regression on two features. The shading is the predicted probability of the orange class, and the dashed line is the 0.5 boundary. Press Step to run gradient descent and watch the cross-entropy fall. Click on the plot to add points of either class and see how the boundary reacts.

example.html:
Interview outcome. The slides fit P(job offered) from CGPA and IQ. With weights 0.4 + 0.3·CGPA − 0.45·IQ, a candidate with CGPA 5 and IQ 6 gets probability 0.31, so the prediction is "No".

Sentiment. A review is turned into six counts (positive words, negative words, "no", pronouns, "!", log length). With the slides' weights the review scores 0.70 probability of being positive.

Supplementary In telecom, the same model estimates the probability that a customer will churn next month from usage, complaints and contract data.

misunderstandings: Logistic regression is a regression method.
It predicts a probability but is used for classification.
Not on imbalanced data; always check recall and precision for the rare class.
Move it to trade false alarms against misses, depending on the cost of each.
In scikit-learn, larger C means stronger regularisation.
It's the opposite: C is the inverse of the penalty strength.
takeaways: Classify by picking the most probable class; mistakes come from overlapping classes.
Logistic regression = weighted score + sigmoid, giving a probability; the boundary is where the score is 0.
Train it with cross-entropy and gradient descent (same update form as linear regression).
Use the confusion matrix, precision, recall and F1, not just accuracy, especially with rare classes.
ROC/AUC compares models across all thresholds; one-vs-rest or one-vs-one handles many classes.
thirty: Logistic regression classifies by computing a weighted score of the inputs and passing it through a sigmoid, giving a probability between 0 and 1; predict yes when it is at least 0.5, which is the same as the score being non-negative. Weights are learned by gradient descent on cross-entropy, which heavily penalises confident mistakes. Each weight multiplies the odds by e to that weight. Judge classifiers with the confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 and ROC/AUC, because accuracy is misleading when one class is rare.

check.q: The sigmoid of a score of 0 is…
check.why: σ(0) = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5, which is why the boundary is where the score is 0.

check.q: Why is least-squares regression a poor classifier?
opts: Outliers shift its threshold and outputs leave the 0–1 range

check.q: A model that always predicts 'no' on 990 no / 10 yes has accuracy…

opts: Of flagged items, how many were right?
Of real positives, how many did we catch?
